title: When Making Requests, Are You Speaking for Yourself or for the Organization
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Distinguishes between requests leaders justify by invoking organizational authority versus those they make personally, arguing the choice carries far more weight than most leaders realize. Organizational appeals let a leader hide behind a faceless institution, making the request easier for team members to deprioritize or resist without it feeling personal. Personal appeals put the leader's own credibility and relationship capital on the line, which the piece argues produces far higher compliance, especially for discretionary asks. The recommended move is to open with the organizational 'why' but pivot the actual ask to come from the leader directly, since resistance to a personal request functionally means the leader has lost credibility.
points: Organizational requests let leaders hide behind a faceless institution, making them easier for team members to dismiss, complain about, or wait out.
Personal requests draw on relationship capital and leadership credibility, making resistance feel like rejecting the leader -- which drives much higher compliance.
Weak leaders lean on institutional framing precisely because it lets them avoid full accountability for the request's reception.
quotes: By using this source of power, leaders position themselves as merely the messenger for assigning the task or making the request, thereby avoiding their full accountability over compliance.
If the team member pushes back to an organizational request, they are resisting the institution, not the leader.
Rejecting or resisting a personal request is tantamount to rejecting the leader. This makes personal requests much more influential and likely to gain acceptance without complaint.
If people do resist, it is often because they don’t respect the leader or hold them as credible, which is why weak leaders often couch their requests as coming from the organization.

For leaders who want team members to go above and beyond, institutional requests fall flat. If the request can be viewed as discretionary in any way, then an organizational plea is more likely to be deflected.
Consider becoming highly intentional about why people should follow your instructions. If they don’t do it for you as a leader, it probably means you aren’t as credible as you need to be.
